I want an O-scope for my shop. What do you know about them? How much should I pay for a decent second hand one? Does old electronic "tools" follow the old adage, "older is better?" ie. USA made Craftsman tools, Bridgeport mills, Monarch Lathes....

It really depends on what you want to do with it. Older electronics, while often works of art as well as science, can be difficult to maintain, worn out, or simply unrepairable as parts break (unless you have a donor unit and the manuals.) Also, remember that in the case of CRT scopes like the classic Tektronix, the CRTs are no longer made and Tek doesn't have the capacity to service them (personal experience asking about one of their last special digital-analog hybrids) any longer. That being said, the old stuff does tend to work, even partially, for a long time, but eventually capacitors are going to dry out, silicon is going to quit as things drift out of tolerance, and switches are going to wear their contacts away.

You're probably going to be looking at $150-200 for a 100MHz brandname model like a Tektronix 465, more if it's one of the modularized units like a Tek 7000 series or one of the fancy newer models with digital displays onscreen. Be aware that a lot of the newer (1990s+) models can often contain obsolete technology like special memory cards, floppy drives, or other peripherals that would be expensive to get or use (GPIB Bubblejet printers anyone?) Lesser known brands like Hitachi, Hickock, B&K Precision, Eico, etc. will command much less money, but you may find they feel a bit cheaper than something from the big players.

If you're just looking for "scope" for the wow factor or to verify waveforms, check the offbrands first. If you need super-precision, the big names will give you better accuracy (but you'll pay for it.) If you have a local hamfest (search your city or area and hamfest) try there, you can play with it and vendors will often demo things for you if electricity is available. Remember you'll probably need some probes.

HOWEVER, if you're looking for something new, Check companies like Rigol (rigolna.com) - they sell some pretty amazing stuff for (relatively) cheap prices. You need to understand that getting service for these can be tricky, so expect to buy their equipment for 5 years and then get a new one. But you really can't beat a full four-channel FFT scope on your bench for well under 10 bills.
